ev.w_old_grandchild_lap.text: Your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} fell asleep in your lap halfway through the story about the wolf. You sat there until dark, afraid to move.
ev.w_old_first_word.text: {npc} said “{g:Grandpa|Grandma}” for the first time — and immediately demanded your bread. The whole family agrees there's a genius in the house.
ev.w_old_needle.text: Your eyes aren't what they were. These days your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter} {npc} threads your needle, with the air of someone granting an enormous favor.
ev.w_old_grandchild_wedding.text: {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:grandson|granddaughter}, got married. You danced at the wedding only once, but in a way the guests talked about all year.
ev.w_old_joints.text.1: Your knees now forecast rain better than any soothsayer. The neighbors laughed at first; now they ask you whether it's safe to hang out the washing.
ev.w_old_joints.text.2: The stairs you ran up all your life without a thought have suddenly grown long. You counted the steps and rested on every fifth one.
ev.w_old_teeth.text: Another tooth gone. Porridge is your favorite food now, and you crack nuts with a stone, grumbling that nuts were softer in your day.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text: The young people at the gate refuse to believe that bread cost half as much in your youth, or that winters were real winters back then. You tell them anyway — and every time, the winters get colder.
ev.w_old_city_changed.text: You walked down the street where you grew up and didn't recognize it: different shops, different voices, even different dogs.
ev.w_old_city_changed.text.rome: Where you once bought nuts from a cross-eyed old woman, there's now a marble portico with a stranger's name on the pediment. It doesn't sell nuts.
ev.w_old_city_changed.text.athens: New statues in the agora, new quarrels, new slang. The boys laugh at your accent, and you laugh at their philosophy.
ev.w_old_city_changed.text.egypt: The new scribe re-registered the whole village and wrote your name in Greek — misspelled. You didn't argue: on a tax list, it's better to be a mistake.
ev.w_old_peer_funeral.text: They buried the neighbor you'd argued with for fifty years over the shared wall. Without his grumbling the street is far too quiet.
ev.w_old_lares.text: {npc} now keeps the household shrine: you placed the sacred things in your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}'s hands yourself and showed where the lamp should burn.
ev.w_old_lares.text.rome: {npc} now keeps the family Lares: you handed over the little bronze figures yourself and explained that on the Kalends, Nones and Ides they get a garland and a drop of wine.
ev.w_old_lares.text.athens: {npc} now keeps the jar of Zeus Ktesios in the storeroom, the god who guards the household's supplies. You showed where it stands and what to say over it.
ev.w_old_lares.text.egypt: {npc} now keeps the family's figure of Bes, the pot-bellied protector god. You handed it over with instructions: put it by the bed whenever a baby is on the way.
ev.w_old_sun_bench.text: A warm wall, the sun, a cup of watered wine and nothing to do until evening. You never knew a person could live like this.
ev.w_tomb_visit.text: You brought wine, honey and flowers to the family tomb and read the names on the stone aloud, so the dead would know they are remembered.
ev.w_old_pass_trade.title: Who takes over
ev.w_old_pass_trade.text: Your hands aren't what they were, and it's time to decide who takes your place. {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}, grew up in the trade — but the apprentice, who isn't family, is sharper and hungrier for the work.
ev.w_old_pass_trade.child.ok: {npc} does everything differently from you. You keep quiet — almost always.
ev.w_old_pass_trade.apprentice.ok: {npc} didn't speak to you for a week. The apprentice brought you the first day's takings — and a pot of honey on top.
ev.w_old_pass_trade.keep: Work as long as you can stand
ev.w_old_pass_trade.keep.ok: Your legs, admittedly, disagree with this decision.
ev.w_old_trade_heir.title: The trade lives on
ev.w_old_trade_heir.text: The trade you handed down didn't wither: {npc} has grown it, hired two workers, and brings you a share at every festival. Nobody has dared take down your old sign.
ev.w_old_apprentice_honor.title: The pupil remembers
ev.w_old_apprentice_honor.text: Your old apprentice is a master now. At the festival he called you his teacher in front of everyone and bowed so low he dropped his garland.
ev.w_old_apprentice_honor.thank: Hug him and shed a tear
ev.w_old_apprentice_honor.grandchild: Ask him to take on one of the youngsters of your family
ev.w_old_apprentice_honor.grandchild.ok: He agreed without a second thought: “Your blood — so the hands will be good too.”
ev.w_old_remarry.title: The matchmaker calls
ev.w_old_remarry.text: The evenings are too quiet in the house. The neighborhood matchmaker hints that a respectable {g:widow|widower} from Potters' Street is lonely too — and is even prepared to put up with your temper.
ev.w_old_remarry.marry.ok: The neighbors gossiped through the whole wedding. And for the first time in years, you slept soundly.
ev.w_old_late_love.title: Late love
ev.w_old_late_love.text: {npc} is the best thing to happen to you in old age: you bicker over fish at the market, then laugh until you cry. Even the relatives have come round.
ev.w_old_retire_rome.title: Out of Rome
ev.w_old_retire_rome.text: Carts rumbling all night, smoke, the endless crush — you can't sleep in Rome anymore. An old acquaintance is selling a cottage with a garden in the Sabine hills, two days' journey away.
ev.w_old_retire_rome.go.ok: The first night you couldn't sleep: too quiet. The second night you slept till noon.
ev.w_old_retire_rome.stay.ok: At least the neighbors are familiar, and the baths are two steps away.
ev.w_old_retire_athens.title: Beneath Hymettus
ev.w_old_retire_athens.text: The city has grown too cramped and noisy for you. At the foot of Mount Hymettus a small plot is for sale: an olive tree, beehives, a well and a view of the sea.
ev.w_old_retire_athens.go.ok: The bees of Hymettus took a while to accept you, but their honey is the best in Attica.
ev.w_old_retire_athens.stay.ok: The agora, the gossip, the theatre — at your age, you don't walk away from that.
ev.w_old_retire_egypt.title: Back to the village
ev.w_old_retire_egypt.text: The city roars, and more and more you dream of a village: a mud-brick wall, a palm tree, the smell of the river after the flood. Your nephew invites you to live out your days with him in the Fayum.
ev.w_old_retire_egypt.go.ok: Your nephew met you at the canal with a donkey and a whole basket of dates.
ev.w_old_retire_egypt.stay.ok: You still dream of the village. Awake, though, the city's doctors are closer.
ev.w_old_country_later.title: Your own fig tree
ev.w_old_country_later.text: You sit in the shade of a fig tree you planted yourself. The neighbors' children are convinced your figs are the best around, and they check regularly.
ev.w_child_quarrel.title: A will of their own
ev.w_child_quarrel.text: At dinner {npc}, your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter}, announces a choice of partner — no matchmaker, no dowry and no asking you. The room goes very quiet.
ev.w_child_quarrel.bless.ok: The wedding was modest. The new in-laws turned out loud, but not unkind.
ev.w_child_quarrel.forbid: Forbid it — or out of the house
ev.w_child_quarrel.forbid.ok: {npc} left that same night. You told everyone you didn't care.
ev.w_child_quarrel.meet: First invite the future in-laws to dinner
ev.w_child_quarrel.meet.success: By the end of the meal you were pouring the in-laws' wine yourself.
ev.w_child_quarrel.meet.failure: Dinner ended in a row about the dowry. {npc} didn't speak to you for a week.
ev.w_old_reconcile.title: Reconciliation
ev.w_old_reconcile.text: {npc} never came home. They say your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} has long had a family of {g=npc_sex:his|her} own, and you have never once crossed {g=npc_sex:his|her} threshold.
ev.w_old_reconcile.go_first.success: You came without gifts or speeches. {npc} stood in the doorway for a long time — then silently stepped aside and let you in.
ev.w_old_reconcile.go_first.failure: They heard you out and closed the door. Maybe later. Maybe never.
ev.w_old_reconcile.letter.ok: A reply came a month later: only three lines, but at the end — "come in the spring."
ev.w_old_reconcile.pride: Whoever left should be the one to come back
ev.w_old_reconcile.pride.ok: The waiting turned out to be longer than you thought.
ev.w_old_tomb.title: A last home
ev.w_old_tomb.text: It's time to think about where you'll lie and what passers-by will read about you. The stonemason is already laying out his samples.
ev.w_old_tomb.text.rome: Along the roads outside the city gates stand tombs inscribed “Stranger, stop and read.” The stonemason offers you a spot as well — with a portrait, your name and a few words about your life.
ev.w_old_tomb.text.athens: In the Kerameikos, along the road out of the city, stand the gravestones of whole families. The stonemason shows samples: from a stele with a farewell handshake to a plain little column bearing a single name.
ev.w_old_tomb.text.egypt: The necropolis craftsmen offer a place in the family tomb and a painted coffin with your name and a prayer to Osiris, so you'll be recognized in the next world.
ev.w_old_tomb.grand: Order a tomb to be proud of
ev.w_old_tomb.grand.ok: The stone came out splendidly. You went to look at it three times, and each time you changed one word of the inscription.
ev.w_old_tomb.modest.rome: Buy a niche in a columbarium
ev.w_old_tomb.modest.ok: Modest, but yours. You feel calmer for it.
ev.w_old_tomb.living: Better spend it on the living
ev.w_old_tomb.living.ok: The neighborhood kids each got a honey cake, and you got their honest opinion that you're the best.
ev.w_rome_salutatio.text: At dawn, clients in rumpled togas crowded outside a senator's house — yawning, clutching little baskets for the handout, letting the better-off go first. In Rome, even the queue for favors has its ranks.
ev.w_rome_baths.text.1: At the baths, for a quarter-as, someone sang at the top of his lungs in the pool, the hair-plucker shouted for customers and the pastry seller out-shouted them both. You came out clean and completely deafened.
ev.w_rome_baths.text.2: At the baths you picked up more news than in a month at the Forum: who's gone bankrupt, who's getting married, and where the baker next door got his new tunic.
ev.w_rome_graffiti.text: Overnight someone painted on the wall of your building in red: “The fruit sellers ask you to elect Lucius aedile.” Underneath, in another hand: “And all the sleepy drunks back Gaius.”
ev.w_rome_sigillaria.text: At the Saturnalia you gave the neighbors' children little clay figures and got a wax candle and a handful of nuts in return. A humble gift, and nobody minds: the festival isn't about the price.
ev.w_rome_saturnalia_slave.text: At the Saturnalia the master poured your wine himself, and the whole household wore felt caps like free people. All evening you didn't know what to do with your hands. Three days later everything was back as it was.
ev.w_rome_appia.text: You traveled down the Via Appia past endless tombs. Their inscriptions speak straight to you: “Traveler, sit and rest a while — and remember me.”
ev.w_rome_frumentatio.text: Once a month, five modii of free grain from the state. The line is long and the clerks check every name on the list, but tonight the house smells of bread.
ev.w_athens_symposium.text: At the symposium the guests took turns singing as they passed the myrtle branch, and one got so carried away at kottabos — flicking wine dregs at a target — that he drenched the host. The master of the feast ordered more water in the mixing bowl.
ev.w_athens_dionysia.text.1: At the Great Dionysia you spent the whole day in the theatre on the slope of the Acropolis: three tragedies in a row and a satyr play. By evening the whole row was crying, the olive seller next to you included.
ev.w_athens_dionysia.text.2: In the comedy an actor in a huge mask mimicked a well-known politician so well that the theatre howled. The politician himself sat in the front rows and laughed loudest of all — just to be safe.
ev.w_athens_gymnasium.text: At the gymnasium under the plane trees, young men oiled themselves and wrestled in the sand, old men argued politics, and some philosopher was asking passers-by what courage is. You left with sand in your ears and a question in your head.
ev.w_athens_thesmophoria.text: For the three days of the Thesmophoria the married women go off to Demeter's sanctuary: they fast, they pray, and then they laugh at jokes their husbands had better never hear. Men aren't allowed in, and they're dying of curiosity.
ev.w_athens_metoikion.text: Freedom in Athens costs money every year: you're a metic now, paying the metic tax, and without a citizen sponsor you can't even go to court.
ev.w_egypt_nilometer.text: The priests announced the reading at the Nilometer: the water has risen sixteen cubits. Sixteen is the best number in the world — all over the district people are roasting geese and dividing up the harvest in advance.
ev.w_egypt_serapis_dream.text: You spent the night in the temple of Sarapis hoping for a prophetic dream. For some reason you dreamed of the neighbor's cow with a basket of dates on her horns. For an obol, the priest explained: an excellent sign.
ev.w_egypt_witnesses.text: You signed a lease on papyrus. The scribe described everyone by their features: “about forty, medium height, honey-colored skin, a scar on the left eyebrow.” It took you a moment to recognize yourself.
ev.w_egypt_crocodile.text.1: Someone saw a crocodile by the canal again. Now the washing is done in threes: two scrub, and the third watches the water and sings loudly, so the beast knows it's been spotted.
ev.w_egypt_crocodile.text.2: In Crocodilopolis the priests pried open the jaws of the sacred crocodile, gold rings in its ears, and like every visitor you dropped in a honey cake. The crocodile accepted it like a god thoroughly tired of pilgrims.
ev.w_egypt_portrait.text: A painter is doing your portrait on a wooden panel in hot wax. When the time comes, it will be laid over your face in the wrappings. You asked him to make you a little younger — he nodded knowingly.
ev.w_egypt_pharos.text: Sailing toward Alexandria, you saw the lighthouse on Pharos for the first time — a white tower taller than any temple. The boatman swears that at night a fire burns at the top, visible far out to sea.
ev.w_egypt_dikes.text: Five days on the dikes — a duty no one escapes. You hauled baskets of silt while the overseer counted them on his fingers and kept losing track.
ev.w_rome_collegium.title: The collegium
ev.w_rome_collegium.text: Your neighbors, all craftsmen, invite you into their collegium: an entrance fee, an amphora of good wine and a few coins every month. In return: dinners on feast days and a decent funeral when your time comes, with a niche in the columbarium and flute players.
ev.w_rome_collegium.note: Roman collegia brought together people of one trade, neighborhood or cult. The charter of a collegium at Lanuvium (AD 136) asked for 100 sesterces and an amphora of good wine on joining, and promised 300 sesterces for the member's funeral. For the poor and for freedmen it was both insurance and a club.
ev.w_rome_collegium.join.ok: At your very first dinner they seated you between a potter and a bath attendant, and by morning you knew all about clay and other people's backs.
ev.w_rome_collegium.decline.ok: Your money's safe. You can think about funerals later.
ev.w_rome_collegium_later.title: Master of the collegium
ev.w_rome_collegium_later.text: The collegium has elected you its master for a year: the dinners, the dues, the sacrifices — and making sure nobody gets drunk before the offering.
ev.w_rome_collegium_later.accept.ok: The dinner you paid for was a triumph. Your name was carved on the marble list of past masters.
ev.w_rome_landlord.title: The landlord
ev.w_rome_landlord.text: The building manager has announced that from the July Kalends the rent goes up by a third. The crack in the wall stays exactly where it is: “It's stood forty years, it'll stand a few more.”
ev.w_rome_landlord.upstairs.ok: Now it's a hundred steps up to your place, but you can see half the city. And hear it too.
ev.w_rome_landlord.sublet: Rent out a corner to a lodger
ev.w_rome_landlord.sublet.success: The lodger turned out to be a quiet copyist who pays in advance.
ev.w_rome_landlord.sublet.failure: The lodger moved out in the night without paying — and took your cloak.
ev.w_rome_landlord.ostia.ok: Ostia smells of sea, fish and money: the harbor always needs hands.
ev.w_rome_election.title: The man in white
ev.w_rome_election.text: A candidate in a chalk-whitened toga shakes your hand and calls you by name — his slave nomenclator whispered it in his ear. His friend quietly adds that there's money for your vote, and a free meal on election day.
ev.w_rome_election.note: The word “candidate” comes from the Latin candidatus, “dressed in white”: men seeking office whitened their togas with chalk. Buying votes was banned by law after law, and flourished anyway. In AD 14, under Tiberius, the election of magistrates was moved from the popular assembly to the Senate.
ev.w_rome_election.take.ok: You took the money. And you voted for him too — a deal's a deal.
ev.w_rome_election.paint: Paint his name on walls for pay
ev.w_rome_election.paint.ok: For a week you painted his name in red. Your letters came out better than his rivals'.
ev.w_rome_ambitus_trial.title: Bribery trial
ev.w_rome_ambitus_trial.text: The candidate who once paid for votes is on trial for bribery. The prosecutor is looking for witnesses — and someone has given him your name.
ev.w_rome_ambitus_trial.testify.ok: You told it as it happened. His friends now greet you through gritted teeth.
ev.w_rome_ambitus_trial.deny.success: You remembered nothing so convincingly that they let you go within a quarter of an hour.
ev.w_rome_ambitus_trial.deny.failure: The prosecutor produced a list of the bribed, and your name was on it. Awkward.
ev.w_rome_candidate_patron.title: The aedile remembers
ev.w_rome_candidate_patron.text: The candidate whose name you painted on the walls became aedile, and he looks after his own: he wants you to keep an eye on the contractors repairing the streets.
ev.w_athens_ostracism.title: The potsherd
ev.w_athens_ostracism.text: Today there's an ostracism in the agora: every citizen scratches on a potsherd the name of the man who should be exiled for ten years. A farmer who can't write holds out his sherd: “Write it for me” — and names a man you respect.
ev.w_athens_ostracism.note: Athens used ostracism from 487 to about 417 BC. If at least 6,000 citizens voted (or, on another reading, if one man got 6,000 votes), the man whose name appeared most often was exiled for ten years, without losing his property. Archaeologists have found thousands of ostraka, including batches clearly prepared in advance by a single hand.
ev.w_athens_ostracism.honest: Write the name he asks for
ev.w_athens_ostracism.honest.ok: You carefully wrote out someone else's decision. The farmer thanked you at length, moving his lips as if reading.
ev.w_athens_ostracism.swap: Write a different name — he can't read anyway
ev.w_athens_ostracism.swap.ok: He can't read and will never know. You, unfortunately, can.
ev.w_athens_farmer_gift.title: Honey from Hymettus
ev.w_athens_farmer_gift.text: At the market the very same farmer with the potsherd called out to you and pressed a jar of honey into your hands: “You wrote it honestly back then — I checked with my son later, he's learned his letters.”
ev.w_athens_jury.title: Juror
ev.w_athens_jury.text: Today you're one of several hundred jurors, and you'll be paid three obols for the day. The defendant is a rich man accused of embezzlement; when his speech ends, he brings his weeping children before the judges.
ev.w_athens_jury.note: Athenian courts (dikasteria) were made up of citizens over 30 chosen by lot — hundreds of men for a single case. Pericles introduced jury pay, and around 425 BC it was raised to three obols. Jurors voted secretly and without deliberation; bringing one's children into court to win pity was a standard tactic.
ev.w_athens_jury.evidence.ok: You felt for the children, but there was a great deal of embezzlement. You cast your vote to convict — and lay awake a long time.
ev.w_athens_jury.pity.ok: He was acquitted. A month later he was seen in a new chariot.
ev.w_athens_jury.bribe: Accept a “gift” from the defendant's friends
ev.w_athens_jury.bribe.success: Nobody noticed a thing. Except you.
ev.w_athens_jury.bribe.failure: The bribe came out, and now your name is repeated in the agora — without any respect.
ev.w_athens_mysteries.title: The Eleusinian Mysteries
ev.w_athens_mysteries.text: Every autumn a procession goes from Athens to Eleusis: thousands of people, torches, piglets for sacrifice — bathed in the sea along with the initiates. Anyone who speaks Greek and has no blood on their hands may be initiated, even a slave. But what you see there, you may never tell.
ev.w_athens_mysteries.note: The Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone at Eleusis were celebrated for over a thousand years. Initiates kept the secret so well that we still don't really know what happened inside the Telesterion. Revealing it was punishable by death; in 415 BC Alcibiades was accused of profaning the Mysteries.
ev.w_athens_mysteries.initiate.ok: You came back at dawn and said nothing all day. Whatever it was, the fear of death has been quieter ever since.
ev.w_athens_mysteries_secret.title: The secret of Eleusis
ev.w_athens_mysteries_secret.text: At dinner with the neighbors, a tipsy friend won't let it go: “Come on, what do they show you in there? I won't tell a soul!” Everyone falls silent and waits.
ev.w_athens_mysteries_secret.joke.succes: You described “Demeter's sacred turnip” so solemnly that the guests laughed till morning.
ev.w_athens_mysteries_secret.joke.failur: The joke was taken as blasphemy. People started saying you mock the goddesses.
ev.w_athens_mysteries_secret.tell.ok: You told. By morning the whole neighborhood knew — and perhaps the goddesses too.
ev.w_athens_piraeus.title: To the Piraeus
ev.w_athens_piraeus.text: A friend is calling you to the Piraeus: grain ships from the Black Sea come in every day, ten languages are spoken on the quays, and there's always work for willing hands. There are also fights in ten languages.
ev.w_athens_piraeus.go.ok: The new house smells of pitch and fish. In the mornings the dockers' shouting wakes you.
ev.w_athens_piraeus_later.title: A share in the cargo
ev.w_athens_piraeus_later.text: After years in the Piraeus you have friends on every quay. A Cypriot merchant offers you a share in a cargo of copper and swears by Aphrodite it's a sure thing.
ev.w_athens_piraeus_later.invest.success: The ship came in safe and the copper sold at a fat price. The merchant didn't swear in vain.
ev.w_athens_piraeus_later.invest.failure: Storms held the ship up and the cargo sold at a loss. Aphrodite was evidently busy.
ev.w_egypt_cat.title: The sacred cat
ev.w_egypt_cat.text: A cat went under the wheel of your cart. In Egypt this is more than bad luck: cats are sacred to the goddess Bastet, and a crowd is already gathering.
ev.w_egypt_cat.note: The Greek historian Diodorus of Sicily writes that he saw with his own eyes an Egyptian crowd kill a Roman who had accidentally killed a cat, and even the king's officials could not save him. Killing a sacred animal was a grave crime, and dead cats were embalmed and buried by the thousands.
ev.w_egypt_cat.confess: Mourn louder than anyone and pay the temple
ev.w_egypt_cat.confess.ok: You wept more convincingly than any hired mourner. The priests accepted your payment, and the cat will be embalmed at your expense.
ev.w_egypt_cat.flee.success: You vanished into the alleys. A pity about the cart — not about you.
ev.w_egypt_cat.flee.failure: They caught you. The bruises will heal; your reputation on the street won't.
ev.w_egypt_cat.lie: Say the cat was already dead
ev.w_egypt_cat.lie.success: They believed you. You don't quite believe yourself.
ev.w_egypt_cat.lie.failure: Someone saw the whole thing, and the crowd stopped listening.
ev.w_egypt_court.title: Two laws
ev.w_egypt_court.text: Your neighbor has grabbed a strip of your field by the canal. You could sue before the Greek judges, the chrematistai — with a hired scribe and speeches — or before the Egyptian laokritai at the temple, by the laws of the ancestors. Or you could make a deal.
ev.w_egypt_court.note: Ptolemaic Egypt had two legal systems: Greeks went to the chrematistai, Egyptians to the laokritai. A decree of 118 BC ruled that the court depended on the language of the contract — Greek or Demotic. After the Roman conquest the courts were reorganized.
ev.w_egypt_court.greek.success: The scribe drafted a flawless complaint, and the judges returned your field with compensation.
ev.w_egypt_court.greek.failure: Your neighbor hired a better scribe. The money's gone and the field is still his.
ev.w_egypt_court.egyptian: The Egyptian court at the temple
ev.w_egypt_court.egyptian.success: The priest-judges heard the village elders and gave you back your field with interest.
ev.w_egypt_court.egyptian.failure: The elders, as luck would have it, remembered everything in your neighbor's favor.
ev.w_egypt_court.settle: Make peace over a jug of beer
ev.w_egypt_court.settle.ok: You split the strip down the middle and drank to the boundary stone.
ev.w_egypt_fayum.title: New land in the Fayum
ev.w_egypt_fayum.text: The kings have drained the marshes of the Fayum, and villages are springing up along the new canals: Greek veterans and Egyptian farmers all mixed together. Land is leased cheaply to anyone not afraid of mosquitoes and hard work.
ev.w_egypt_fayum.note: Under Ptolemy II Philadelphus huge areas of the Fayum were drained and irrigated, and veteran soldiers (cleruchs) were given plots there. Dozens of villages grew up — Philadelphia, Karanis, Tebtunis. Thousands of papyri from them are our main source for everyday life in Hellenistic and Roman Egypt.
ev.w_egypt_fayum.go.ok: The first thing you bought was a mosquito net. The second was a hoe.
ev.w_egypt_fayum_later.title: The canal silts up
ev.w_egypt_fayum_later.text: The canal that waters your village gets shallower every year. The headman calls everyone to clear it together — or each can save his own plot alone.
ev.w_egypt_fayum_later.together.ok: Two weeks knee-deep in silt — but the water flows again, and the harvest was good.
ev.w_egypt_fayum_later.alone.success: Your channel worked better than the shared one. The neighbors are jealous.
ev.w_egypt_fayum_later.alone.failure: The first water washed your channel out. You had to go hat in hand to the headman.
ev.w_egypt_alexandria_move.title: To Alexandria
ev.w_egypt_alexandria_move.text: Your cousin writes from Alexandria: “The streets are straight as a stretched thread, the lighthouse is taller than mountains, and a shop on the Canopic Way needs a worker. Come — in the village you'll grow old over the same ditch.”
ev.w_egypt_alexandria_move.go.ok: The city deafened you from the first day: everyone talks at once, in every language, and everyone haggles.
ev.w_egypt_alexandria_later.title: A true Alexandrian
ev.w_egypt_alexandria_later.text: You're a real Alexandrian now: you haggle in two languages, know where to get the best roasted chickpeas, and argue about the races at the hippodrome.
ev.w_egypt_mummify.title: The last journey
ev.w_egypt_mummify.text: Your old uncle, who taught you to fish, has died. The embalmers offer everything from the expensive way — with spices and seventy days' work — to the simple one: natron and linen.
ev.w_egypt_mummify.note: Herodotus describes three grades of embalming, from the most costly to the very simple. The custom outlived every change of rulers: under the Ptolemies and the Romans both Egyptians and many Greeks were mummified, and from the 1st century AD in the Fayum, portraits painted in wax were placed over the mummies' faces.
ev.w_egypt_mummify.full.ok: Your uncle was sent off in a way the neighbors talked about for a year. You're sure he would have approved.
ev.w_egypt_mummify.simple.ok: There was no more money. You asked your uncle's forgiveness for a long time.
ev.w_g_twelve_tables.title: The Twelve Tables
ev.w_g_twelve_tables.text: The laws, written on twelve tablets, have been put on display in the Forum. Now anyone who can read can find out what is allowed and what isn't, instead of taking the patricians' word for it.
ev.w_g_twelve_tables.note: According to Roman tradition, in 451–450 BC a board of ten men, the decemvirs, wrote down the laws of the Twelve Tables. The original does not survive: the text is known from quotations in later authors, and many details are scholarly reconstructions.
ev.w_g_gauls.title: Gauls in Rome
ev.w_g_gauls.text: The Gauls have routed the Roman army at the river Allia and entered the city. Whoever can is fleeing to neighboring towns or taking refuge on the Capitol, while smoke rises over the rooftops.
ev.w_g_gauls.note: Around 390 BC (387/386 BC according to Polybius) Gauls led by Brennus defeated the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome. The stories of the geese that woke the Capitol's defenders and of the words “Woe to the vanquished!” come from much later authors and are probably embellished.
ev.w_g_gauls.capitol.success: The Capitol held, and so did you. The Gauls left after being paid off in gold.
ev.w_g_gauls.capitol.failure: Months of siege broke your health, and meanwhile your house was plundered.
ev.w_g_gracchi.title: Tiberius Gracchus
ev.w_g_gracchi.text: The tribune Tiberius Gracchus wanted to give public land to the poor. On election day senators and their followers attacked him near the Capitol: he and hundreds of his supporters were killed.
ev.w_g_gracchi.note: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, tribune in 133 BC, passed a law redistributing public land and was killed along with about three hundred supporters. His brother Gaius continued the reforms and died in 121 BC. Many historians date the century of Roman civil wars from the Gracchi.
ev.w_g_augustus.title: Augustus
ev.w_g_augustus.text: The Senate has given Octavian a new name — Augustus, “the revered.” He says he has restored the Republic, yet somehow everyone just calls him the princeps. What matters is that the wars seem to be over.
ev.w_g_augustus.note: On 16 January 27 BC the Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus. The Republic survived in form, but one-man rule — the Principate — had in fact begun. The doors of the temple of Janus, closed only in peacetime, were closed three times under Augustus.
ev.w_g_vesuvius.title: Vesuvius
ev.w_g_vesuvius.text: Terrible news arrives from the south: Vesuvius has woken, and Pompeii and Herculaneum lie buried in ash. Refugees from Campania are begging for bread and shelter at the city gates.
ev.w_g_vesuvius.note: The eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 destroyed Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae. Pliny the Younger's letters give 24 August, though some finds point to the autumn. Pliny the Elder, commanding the fleet at Misenum, died; the emperor Titus provided money for the victims.
ev.w_g_colosseum.title: The Flavian Amphitheatre
ev.w_g_colosseum.text: The emperor Titus has opened an enormous new amphitheatre: a hundred days of games, beast hunts and even a sea battle on a flooded arena. The city talks of nothing else.
ev.w_g_colosseum.note: The Flavian Amphitheatre, later nicknamed the Colosseum, was begun by Vespasian around AD 70–72 and opened by Titus in 80. Suetonius and Cassius Dio describe a hundred days of games; according to Dio, at the opening the arena was flooded for a naval battle.
ev.w_g_colosseum.stay: Work while everyone's at the games
ev.w_g_parthenon.title: The Parthenon
ev.w_g_parthenon.text: A new temple of Athena is going up on the Acropolis. The city is full of stonecutters, carters hauling Pentelic marble and Phidias' craftsmen: there's work for everyone, and the arguments over whose money is paying for it never stop.
ev.w_g_parthenon.note: The Parthenon was built from 447 to 438 BC, and its sculpture was finished by 432. Phidias oversaw the work; the architects were Ictinus and Callicrates. Pericles' building programme was partly funded from the treasury of the Delian League, which caused controversy even in Athens.
ev.w_g_parthenon.work: Hire on at the building site
ev.w_g_parthenon.work.ok: All season you dressed marble. On one block you secretly cut a tiny mark of your own.
ev.w_g_parthenon.admire: Go and watch the walls rise
ev.w_parthenon_stone.title: My stone
ev.w_parthenon_stone.text: You took the youngsters up the Acropolis and showed them a block in the temple wall with the tiny mark you once cut yourself. They didn't believe you — but they listened until evening.
ev.w_g_thirty.title: The Thirty Tyrants
ev.w_g_thirty.text: After the defeat in the war, the Spartans have set the Thirty over Athens. They execute the rich and the inconvenient and seize their property; citizens are fleeing to Thebes.
ev.w_g_thirty.note: In 404 BC the Thirty, led by Critias, ruled Athens backed by a Spartan garrison; according to Aristotle they executed about 1,500 people. In 403 the democrats under Thrasybulus, starting from the mountain fort of Phyle, took back power, and Athens declared one of the first amnesties in history.
ev.w_g_thirty.phyle: Join the exiles at the fort of Phyle
ev.w_g_thirty.phyle.success: Thrasybulus' men marched back into the city victorious, and you were in their ranks.
ev.w_g_thirty.phyle.failure: You were wounded in a skirmish near the Piraeus. Democracy won; the scar remained.
ev.w_g_socrates.title: The death of Socrates
ev.w_g_socrates.text: The court has sentenced Socrates to death — that odd fellow who pestered everyone in the agora with questions. The charge: impiety and corrupting the young. They say he refused to escape from prison, though his friends had arranged everything.
ev.w_g_socrates.note: In 399 BC a jury of 501 found Socrates guilty of impiety and corrupting the youth, and he drank poison — hemlock. His trial and death were described by his pupils Plato and Xenophon, so we see them through their eyes.
ev.w_g_socrates.wrong: The city has killed a wise man
ev.w_g_socrates.deserved: He led the young astray and angered the gods
ev.w_g_socrates.silent: Better not to say it aloud
ev.w_g_chaeronea.title: Chaeronea
ev.w_g_chaeronea.text: At Chaeronea King Philip of Macedon has crushed the Athenians and Thebans; his cavalry was led by his eighteen-year-old son, Alexander. The city braced for a siege — but Philip released the prisoners without ransom.
ev.w_g_chaeronea.note: The battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC ended the independence of the Greek city-states in the face of Macedon. Philip II treated Athens leniently: he returned the prisoners without ransom and installed no garrison. The funeral speech for the fallen was given by Demosthenes.
ev.w_g_hadrian_athens.title: Hadrian in Athens
ev.w_g_hadrian_athens.text: The emperor Hadrian is in Athens again: he has been initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries, is building a library and is at last finishing the temple of Olympian Zeus, which has stood incomplete for over six centuries.
ev.w_g_hadrian_athens.note: Hadrian visited Athens in 124/125, 128/129 and 131/132 AD. He completed the Olympieion, begun under the Peisistratids in the 6th century BC, and built a library and a new quarter. The arch at the quarter's edge reads “This is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus” on one side and “This is the city of Hadrian, not of Theseus” on the other.
ev.w_g_hadrian_athens.work: Hire on at the imperial works
ev.w_g_hadrian_athens.watch: Watch the emperor and his retinue
ev.w_g_pharos.title: The Pharos lighthouse
ev.w_g_pharos.text: At the mouth of Alexandria's harbor the lighthouse on the island of Pharos has been finished — a white tower of several tiers, taller than any temple. They say it can be seen from far out at sea.
ev.w_g_pharos.note: The lighthouse was built by Sostratus of Cnidus under Ptolemy I and Ptolemy II and finished around 280 BC, though the exact date is disputed. Its height is estimated at over 100 meters. It was counted among the Seven Wonders of the World and stood until the earthquakes of the 14th century.
ev.w_g_rosetta.title: The priests' decree
ev.w_g_rosetta.text: A stone stele has been set up in the temple: a council of priests at Memphis thanks the young king Ptolemy V for gifts to the temples and for forgiving tax arrears. The text is carved three times — in sacred signs, in Demotic and in Greek, so that everyone can read it.
ev.w_g_rosetta.note: The Memphis Decree of 196 BC was copied on stelae across the country. One copy, found at Rosetta in 1799, helped Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822: the Greek text was the key.
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.title: War in Alexandria
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.text: There's fighting in the streets of Alexandria: Caesar is shut in the palace quarter with Cleopatra, facing her brother's army and half the city. Ships are burning in the harbor, and the fire has spread to the warehouses on the quay.
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.note: The Alexandrian War of 48–47 BC. Caesar set fire to the ships in the harbor and the flames spread to buildings by the docks. Ancient writers speak of burned books — from 40,000 scrolls in warehouses to the whole Library — but the scale of the loss is disputed: the Library apparently kept working afterward.
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.hide: Wait it out behind a locked door
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.fight_fire: Fight the fire on the quay
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.fight_fire.succ: The warehouse you saved belonged to a rich merchant. He remembered your face.
ev.w_g_caesar_alexandria.fight_fire.fail: A burning beam crashed down right next to you. The burns took a long time to heal.
ev.w_g_antinous.title: Antinous
ev.w_g_antinous.text: The emperor Hadrian was sailing up the Nile when his young favorite Antinous drowned. The emperor is grief-stricken: a new city, Antinoopolis, is to be built where he died, and the youth is to be worshipped as a god.
ev.w_g_antinous.note: Antinous drowned in the Nile in October AD 130; the circumstances are unclear — accident, sacrifice or suicide. Hadrian founded Antinoopolis at the spot, and the cult of Antinous spread throughout the empire.
ev.w_g_kitos.title: The Diaspora revolt
ev.w_g_kitos.text: The Jewish communities of Egypt, Cyrenaica and Cyprus have risen against the Romans and their Greek neighbors. Villages are burning, troops march along the roads, and in Alexandria yesterday's neighbors fear one another.
ev.w_g_kitos.note: The revolt of AD 115–117 spread across Egypt, Cyrenaica and Cyprus and was brutally put down by Trajan's troops. The Jewish community of Alexandria, one of the largest in the ancient world, almost vanished for a century afterward. Eusebius, Cassius Dio and Egyptian papyri describe these events.
ev.w_g_kitos.shelter: Shelter neighbors who are in danger
ev.w_g_kitos.shelter.success: You sat out the worst days together. That is something no one forgets.
ev.w_g_kitos.shelter.failure: Your house was searched and looted, but you got your neighbors out over the roof in time.
